claim: Rice dwarf virus (RDV) is a member of the genus Phytoreovirus in the family Reoviridae.
source: Rice dwarf virus (RDV), a member of the genus Phytoreovirus in the family Reoviridae, is one of the most widespread and devastating viruses that infect rice (Wu et al., 2015; Jin et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wu et al., 2015 and Jin et al., 2016

claim: RDV is one of the most widespread and devastating viruses that infect rice.
source: Rice dwarf virus (RDV), a member of the genus Phytoreovirus in the family Reoviridae, is one of the most widespread and devastating viruses that infect rice (Wu et al., 2015; Jin et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wu et al., 2015 and Jin et al., 2016

claim: RDV is transovarially transmitted by the green rice leafhopper (Nephotettix cincticeps) in a persistent-propagative manner.
source: RDV is transovarially transmitted by the green rice leafhopper (Nephotettix cincticeps) in a persistent-propagative manner (Cao et al., 2005; Zhou et al., 2007; Wei and Li, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cao et al., 2005; Zhou et al., 2007; Wei and Li, 2016

claim: RDV infection greatly inhibits rice growth and causes severe symptoms including dwarfism, increased tillering, and white chlorotic specks and dark-green discoloration on the leaves.
source: RDV infection greatly inhibits rice growth and causes severe symptoms including dwarfism, increased tillering, and white chlorotic specks and dark-green discoloration on the leaves.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about RDV symptoms based on established knowledge

claim: RDV has a double-stranded RNA genome consisting of 12 segments (S1 to S12).
source: RDV has a double-stranded RNA genome consisting of 12 segments (S1 to S12).
evidence: Supported by citations in the following sentence

claim: Seven RDV segments (S1, S2, S3, S5, S7, S8, and S9) encode structural proteins P1, P2, P3, P5, P7, P8, and P9, respectively, which form double-layered virions.
source: Seven segments, S1, S2, S3, S5, S7, S8, and S9, encode structural proteins P1, P2, P3, P5, P7, P8, and P9, respectively, which form double-layered virions; the remaining segments, S4, S6, S10, S11, and S12, encode the nonstructural proteins Pns4, Pns6, Pns10, Pns11, and Pns12 (Cao et al., 2005; Zhou et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2014; Jin et al., 2016; Wei and Li, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cao et al., 2005; Zhou et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2014; Jin et al., 2016; Wei and Li, 2016

claim: The remaining RDV segments (S4, S6, S10, S11, and S12) encode the nonstructural proteins Pns4, Pns6, Pns10, Pns11, and Pns12.
source: Seven segments, S1, S2, S3, S5, S7, S8, and S9, encode structural proteins P1, P2, P3, P5, P7, P8, and P9, respectively, which form double-layered virions; the remaining segments, S4, S6, S10, S11, and S12, encode the nonstructural proteins Pns4, Pns6, Pns10, Pns11, and Pns12 (Cao et al., 2005; Zhou et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2014; Jin et al., 2016; Wei and Li, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cao et al., 2005; Zhou et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2014; Jin et al., 2016; Wei and Li, 2016

claim: RDV-encoded Pns11 protein was previously found to function as a component of viroplasms.
source: RDV-encoded Pns11 protein was previously found to function as a component of viroplasms (Wei et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wei et al., 2006

claim: Overexpression of Pns11 in rice enhances susceptibility to RDV infection.
source: To investigate whether Pns11 plays an important role in RDV infection, transgenes encoding Pns11 were introduced into the rice cultivar Zhonghua 11 to generate Pns11-overexpression plants, referred to as S11 OX lines hereafter.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1, including symptoms, northern blot, western blot, and infection rates

claim: At four weeks post inoculation (4 wpi), the S11 OX lines exhibited more severe RDV infection symptoms with more stunting and chlorotic flecks on the leaves than the WT control plants.
source: At four weeks post inoculation (4 wpi), the S11 OX lines exhibited more severe RDV infection symptoms with more stunting and chlorotic flecks on the leaves than the WT control plants (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by visual data in Figure 1A showing disease symptoms

claim: RDV RNA genome segments showed increased accumulation in two of the S11 OX lines (except S11 OX#3) relative to the WT plants.
source: Three RDV RNA genome segments and their encoded proteins were evaluated by northern and western blot assays. The results showed increased accumulation in two of the S11 OX lines (except S11 OX#3) relative to the WT plants (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by northern blot data in Figure 1B

claim: RDV-encoded proteins showed increased accumulation in two of the S11 OX lines (except S11 OX#3) relative to the WT plants.
source: Three RDV RNA genome segments and their encoded proteins were evaluated by northern and western blot assays. The results showed increased accumulation in two of the S11 OX lines (except S11 OX#3) relative to the WT plants (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 1C

claim: The infection rates were higher in the S11 OX#5 and S11 OX#11 lines than in the WT.
source: In addition, the infection rates were higher in the S11 OX#5 and S11 OX#11 lines than in the the WT (Figure 1D, Supplementary file 2A).
evidence: Supported by infection rate data in Figure 1D

claim: Pns11 specifically interacts with OsSAMS1 in yeast two-hybrid assays.
source: This screen identified OsSAMS1 as a strong interaction partner of Pns11. The rice genome encodes three members of the predicted SAMS family, OsSAMS1, OsSAMS2, and OsSAMS3, which show high levels of sequence identity in their DNA and deduced amino acid sequences (Li et al., 2011). However, Pns11 only interacted with OsSAMS1, and not with OsSAMS2 or OsSAMS3 in yeast.
evidence: Supported by yeast two-hybrid data in Figure 2A

claim: OsSAMS1 specifically interacted with Pns11, but not with other RDV-encoded proteins.
source: Moreover, OsSAMS1 specifically interacted with Pns11, but not with other RDV-encoded proteins (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by yeast two-hybrid data in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Pns11 and OsSAMS1 interact in Co-IP assays in N. benthamiana leaves.
source: To further test this specific interaction in plant cells, we performed a co-IP experiment by co-expressing hemagglutinin (HA)-epitope-tagged Pns11 and FLAG-tagged OsSAMS1, OsSAMS2, or OsSAMS3 in a transient expression assay in Nicotiana benthamiana leaves, followed by immunoprecipitation with FLAG-tag antibodies and HA-tag antibodies (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by Co-IP data in Figure 2B

claim: Pns11 and OsSAMS1 interact in firefly luciferase complementation imaging assays.
source: We further verified this interaction using a firefly luciferase (LUC) complementation imaging assay. Constructs encoding Pns11 fused with the N-terminus of LUC (Pns11-nLUC) and the C-terminus of LUC fused with OsSAMS1 (cLUC-OsSAMS1) were co-infiltrated into N. benthamiana leaves for transient co-expression of these two fusion proteins. A luminescence signal was only detected in Pns11-nLUC/cLUC-OsSAMS1 co-expression regions but not in the negative controls (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by luciferase complementation data in Figure 2C

claim: Pns11 and OsSAMS1 interact in vivo in RDV-infected rice cells.
source: Finally, we also performed a in vivo pull-down assay with whole-cell lysates from non-infected controls and RDV-infected rice plants and found that Pns11 and OsSAMS1 interacted in RDV-infected rice cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by in vivo pull-down data in Figure 2D

claim: Pns11 and OsSAMS1 are co-localized in both nucleus and cytoplasm.
source: Bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC) analysis also demonstrated that Pns11 and OsSAMS1 interacted and were co-localized in both nucleus and cytoplasm (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by BiFC data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: The OsSAMS1 mRNA level did not change in response to Pns11 overexpression.
source: We used S11 OX rice tissues at three stages (5-leaf, 6-leaf, and 10-leaf stage) for real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) measurements and western blot. The OsSAMS1 mRNA and OsSAMS1 protein level did not change in response to Pns11 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D

claim: The OsSAMS1 protein level did not change in response to Pns11 overexpression.
source: We used S11 OX rice tissues at three stages (5-leaf, 6-leaf, and 10-leaf stage) for real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) measurements and western blot. The OsSAMS1 mRNA and OsSAMS1 protein level did not change in response to Pns11 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E

claim: SAMS catalyzes the conversion of L-methionine (L-Met) and ATP into S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM).
source: In plants, S-adenosyl-L-methionine synthetase (SAMS) [EC 2.5.1.6] catalyzes the conversion of L-methionine (L-Met) and ATP into S-adenosyl-L-methionine (AdoMet, SAM), which serves as a precursor of ethylene and polyamines.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about SAMS enzyme function

claim: SAM serves as a precursor of ethylene and polyamines.
source: In plants, S-adenosyl-L-methionine synthetase (SAMS) [EC 2.5.1.6] catalyzes the conversion of L-methionine (L-Met) and ATP into S-adenosyl-L-methionine (AdoMet, SAM), which serves as a precursor of ethylene and polyamines.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about SAM's role in biosynthesis

claim: The enzymatic activity of OsSAMS1 was enhanced by nearly 60% at a 6:1 molar ratio of Pns11:OsSAMS1.
source: The enzymatic activity of OsSAMS1 was enhanced by nearly 60% at a 6:1 molar ratio of Pns11:OsSAMS1 (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by in vitro enzyme activity assay data in Figure 2G and 2H

claim: Neither P9 nor GFP affected OsSAMS1 activity at the same molar ratio as Pns11:OsSAMS1.
source: In the two negative control reactions with the same molar ratio of Pns11:OsSAMS1, neither P9 nor GFP affected OsSAMS1 activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by negative control data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: Pns11 did not affect OsSAMS2 enzymatic activity.
source: In addition, Pns11 did not affect OsSAMS2 enzymatic activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by enzyme activity assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: SAM content increased in two of the S11 OX lines (but not in S11 OX#3).
source: S11 OX lines were used for analysis and the results showed that SAM, ACC and ethylene contents increased in two of the S11 OX lines (but not in S11 OX#3) (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: Supported by SAM measurement data in Figure 3A

claim: ACC content increased in two of the S11 OX lines (but not in S11 OX#3).
source: S11 OX lines were used for analysis and the results showed that SAM, ACC and ethylene contents increased in two of the S11 OX lines (but not in S11 OX#3) (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: Supported by ACC measurement data in Figure 3B

claim: Ethylene content increased in two of the S11 OX lines (but not in S11 OX#3).
source: S11 OX lines were used for analysis and the results showed that SAM, ACC and ethylene contents increased in two of the S11 OX lines (but not in S11 OX#3) (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: Supported by ethylene measurement data in Figure 3C

claim: Seed germination was suppressed in the OsSAMS1 RNAi and KO lines.
source: Seed germination was suppressed in the OsSAMS1 RNAi and KO lines and the suppression could be rescued by supplementation with SAM and ethylene (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by seed germination data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E

claim: Suppression of seed germination in OsSAMS1 RNAi and KO lines could be rescued by supplementation with SAM and ethylene.
source: Seed germination was suppressed in the OsSAMS1 RNAi and KO lines and the suppression could be rescued by supplementation with SAM and ethylene (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E

claim: The RNAi and KO lines showed developmental defects, including dwarfism and reduced fertility.
source: The RNAi and KO lines also showed developmental defects, including dwarfism and reduced fertility (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F) (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by phenotypic data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and citation to Li et al., 2011

claim: SAM content increased in the OsSAMS1 OX lines and decreased in the OsSAMS1 RNAi and KO lines.
source: In our study, SAM, ACC, and ethylene contents all increased in the OsSAMS1 OX lines and decreased in the OsSAMS1 RNAi and KO lines (Figure 3D–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by SAM measurement data in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A

claim: ACC content increased in the OsSAMS1 OX lines and decreased in the OsSAMS1 RNAi and KO lines.
source: In our study, SAM, ACC, and ethylene contents all increased in the OsSAMS1 OX lines and decreased in the OsSAMS1 RNAi and KO lines (Figure 3D–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by ACC measurement data in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B

claim: Ethylene content increased in the OsSAMS1 OX lines and decreased in the OsSAMS1 RNAi and KO lines.
source: In our study, SAM, ACC, and ethylene contents all increased in the OsSAMS1 OX lines and decreased in the OsSAMS1 RNAi and KO lines (Figure 3D–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by ethylene measurement data in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C

claim: All three OsSAMS1 OX lines displayed more severe stunting symptoms and chlorotic flecks at the infection site than the WT control plants at 4 wpi.
source: At 4 wpi, all three OX lines displayed more severe stunting symptoms and chlorotic flecks at the infection site than the WT control plants, suggesting that they were more susceptible to RDV infection, while the RNAi and KO lines showed greater tolerance (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by symptom data in Figure 4A

claim: The OsSAMS1 RNAi and KO lines showed greater tolerance to RDV infection than WT at 4 wpi.
source: At 4 wpi, all three OX lines displayed more severe stunting symptoms and chlorotic flecks at the infection site than the WT control plants, suggesting that they were more susceptible to RDV infection, while the RNAi and KO lines showed greater tolerance (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by symptom data in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: RDV accumulation was higher in the OsSAMS1 OX lines than in the WT, but much lower in the RNAi and KO lines.
source: Northern and western blot assays revealed that RDV accumulation was higher in the OX lines than in the WT, but much lower in the RNAi and KO lines (Figure 4B,C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by northern and western blot data in Figure 4B,C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C

claim: The infection rate was higher in the OsSAMS1 OX lines, but much lower in the RNAi and KO lines compared to the WT plants.
source: The infection rate was also higher in the OX lines, but much lower in the RNAi and KO lines compared to the WT plants (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, Supplementary file 2B, C).
evidence: Supported by infection rate data in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D

claim: The rice MHZ7 gene (named OsEIN2) encodes a membrane protein homologous to EIN2, a central component of ethylene signaling in Arabidopsis.
source: The rice MHZ7 gene (named OsEIN2), which encodes a membrane protein homologous to EIN2, a central component of ethylene signaling in Arabidopsis, also plays a key role in the rice ethylene signaling pathway (Ma et al., 2013; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ma et al., 2013 and Li et al., 2015

claim: OsEIN2 plays a key role in the rice ethylene signaling pathway.
source: The rice MHZ7 gene (named OsEIN2), which encodes a membrane protein homologous to EIN2, a central component of ethylene signaling in Arabidopsis, also plays a key role in the rice ethylene signaling pathway (Ma et al., 2013; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ma et al., 2013 and Li et al., 2015

claim: The ethylene signaling mutant mhz7 (osein2) is insensitive to ethylene in both the root and coleoptile.
source: The ethylene signaling mutant mhz7 (osein2) is insensitive to ethylene in both the root and coleoptile.
evidence: This is a characterization of the mutant phenotype based on established knowledge

claim: The OsEIN2 OX#2 and OX#3 lines showed enhanced susceptibility with more severe stunting and chlorotic flecks on the leaves than did the WT control plants at 4 wpi.
source: At 4 wpi, the OsEIN2 OX#2 and OX#3 lines showed enhanced susceptibility with more severe stunting and chlorotic flecks on the leaves than did the WT control plants. By contrast, the osein2 mutant showed much milder dwarfism and fewer chlorotic flecks on the leaves (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by symptom data in Figure 5A

claim: The osein2 mutant showed much milder dwarfism and fewer chlorotic flecks on the leaves than WT at 4 wpi.
source: At 4 wpi, the OsEIN2 OX#2 and OX#3 lines showed enhanced susceptibility with more severe stunting and chlorotic flecks on the leaves than did the WT control plants. By contrast, the osein2 mutant showed much milder dwarfism and fewer chlorotic flecks on the leaves (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by symptom data in Figure 5A

claim: RDV accumulation was much higher in the OsEIN2 OX lines than in the WT plants, but lower in the mutant lines.
source: Northern and western blot assays indicated that RDV accumulation was much higher in the OsEIN2 OX lines than in the WT plants, but lower in the mutant lines (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: Supported by northern and western blot data in Figure 5B,C

claim: At 8 wpi, the infection rate of the osein2 mutant was only 43%, which was significantly lower than that of the WT (84%) and the OsEIN2 OX lines (OX#2, 96%; OX#3, 99%).
source: At 8 wpi, the infection rate of the osein2 mutant was only 43%, which was significantly lower than that of the WT (84%) and the OsEIN2 OX lines (OX#2, 96%; OX#3, 99%) (Figure 5D, Supplementary file 2D).
evidence: Supported by infection rate data in Figure 5D

claim: The J119 lines, as well as the parental osein2 mutant, were less susceptible to RDV than was WT rice at 4 wpi.
source: Four weeks post inoculation, we found that the J119 lines, as well as the parental osein2 mutant, were less susceptible to RDV than was WT rice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 1E, Supplementary file 2E).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: The loss of Pns11-OsSAMS1 interaction occurred in Ossams1 KO lines, with or without RDV infection.
source: We first performed a pull-down assay in WT and Ossams1 KO lines, with and without RDV infection, using an anti-OsSAMS1 antibody (Figure 6A). We found the loss of Pns11-OsSAMS1 interaction in Ossams1 KO lines, with or without RDV infection.
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data in Figure 6A

claim: The RDV-induced increase of SAM, ACC and ethylene levels disappeared in Ossams1 KO plants.
source: We then measured the SAM, ACC and ethylene levels in the same set of plants, and found that the RDV-induced increase of SAM, ACC and ethylene levels disappeared in Ossams1 KO plants (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: Supported by SAM, ACC, and ethylene measurement data in Figure 6B-D

claim: Known ethylene-activated pathway genes were highly enriched in both RDV-infected and OsSAMS1 OX transgenic rice, and depleted in Ossams1 KO plants.
source: To determine whether the ethylene pathway was activated, Gene Ontology (GO) was used for analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). Known ethylene-activated pathway genes were highly enriched in both RDV-infected and OsSAMS1 OX transgenic rice, and depleted in Ossams1 KO plants.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq and GO analysis data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: OsERF3 was significantly upregulated by ACC treatment and significantly downregulated by AVG treatment when compared to the H2O-treated control.
source: We then sampled the treated plants and used qRT-PCR to analyze the expression of OsERF3, which could be a marker for the response to ethylene (Qi et al., 2011). OsERF3 was significantly upregulated by ACC treatment and significantly downregulated by AVG treatment when compared to the H2O-treated control (Figure 6E), demonstrating that the ACC and AVG treatments worked as expected.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 6E

claim: The ACC-treated plants showed greater susceptibility to RDV infection, displaying more severe disease symptoms and virus accumulation than the RDV-infected plants treated with H2O at 4 wpi.
source: At 4 wpi, the ACC-treated plants showed greater susceptibility to RDV infection, displaying more severe disease symptoms and virus accumulation than the RDV-infected plants treated with H2O. However, the AVG-treated plants exhibited enhanced disease tolerance, as shown by less virus accumulation and milder disease symptoms, when compared with the RDV-infected plants treated with H2O (Figure 6F–H).
evidence: Supported by symptom and virus accumulation data in Figure 6F-H

claim: The AVG-treated plants exhibited enhanced disease tolerance, as shown by less virus accumulation and milder disease symptoms, when compared with the RDV-infected plants treated with H2O at 4 wpi.
source: At 4 wpi, the ACC-treated plants showed greater susceptibility to RDV infection, displaying more severe disease symptoms and virus accumulation than the RDV-infected plants treated with H2O. However, the AVG-treated plants exhibited enhanced disease tolerance, as shown by less virus accumulation and milder disease symptoms, when compared with the RDV-infected plants treated with H2O (Figure 6F–H).
evidence: Supported by symptom and virus accumulation data in Figure 6F-H

claim: The rate of RDV infection in the ACC-treated plants increased much faster than that in the RDV-infected H2O-treated plants.
source: In addition, the rate of RDV infection in the ACC-treated plants increased much faster than that in the RDV-infected H2O-treated plants, while the rate of infection in the AVG-treated plants increased more slowly in comparison with that in the H2O-treated plants (Figure 6I, Supplementary file 2F).
evidence: Supported by infection rate data in Figure 6I

claim: The rate of infection in the AVG-treated plants increased more slowly in comparison with that in the H2O-treated plants.
source: In addition, the rate of RDV infection in the ACC-treated plants increased much faster than that in the RDV-infected H2O-treated plants, while the rate of infection in the AVG-treated plants increased more slowly in comparison with that in the H2O-treated plants (Figure 6I, Supplementary file 2F).
evidence: Supported by infection rate data in Figure 6I

claim: RDV infection triggers ethylene production by stimulating the activity of S-adenosyl-L-methionine synthetase (SAMS).
source: Here, we report that Rice dwarf virus (RDV) triggers ethylene production by stimulating the activity of S-adenosyl-L-methionine synthetase (SAMS), a key component of the ethylene synthesis pathway, resulting in elevated susceptibility to RDV.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by multiple experimental results throughout the manuscript

claim: RDV-encoded Pns11 protein specifically interacted with OsSAMS1 to enhance its enzymatic activity.
source: RDV-encoded Pns11 protein specifically interacted with OsSAMS1 to enhance its enzymatic activity, leading to higher ethylene levels in both RDV-infected and Pns11-overexpressing rice.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by interaction and enzyme activity assays in Figures 2 and 3

claim: Pns11-overexpressing rice were substantially more susceptible to RDV infection.
source: Consistent with a counter-defense role for ethylene, Pns11-overexpressing rice, as well as those overexpressing OsSAMS1, were substantially more susceptible to RDV infection, and a similar effect was observed in rice plants treated with an ethylene precursor.
evidence: Supported by infection data in Figure 1

claim: Rice overexpressing OsSAMS1 were substantially more susceptible to RDV infection.
source: Consistent with a counter-defense role for ethylene, Pns11-overexpressing rice, as well as those overexpressing OsSAMS1, were substantially more susceptible to RDV infection, and a similar effect was observed in rice plants treated with an ethylene precursor.
evidence: Supported by infection data in Figure 4

claim: Rice plants treated with an ethylene precursor were substantially more susceptible to RDV infection.
source: Consistent with a counter-defense role for ethylene, Pns11-overexpressing rice, as well as those overexpressing OsSAMS1, were substantially more susceptible to RDV infection, and a similar effect was observed in rice plants treated with an ethylene precursor.
evidence: Supported by ACC treatment data in Figure 6

claim: OsSAMS1-knockout mutants resisted RDV infection more robustly.
source: Conversely, OsSAMS1-knockout mutants, as well as an osein2 mutant defective in ethylene signaling, resisted RDV infection more robustly.
evidence: Supported by infection data in Figure 4

claim: An osein2 mutant defective in ethylene signaling resisted RDV infection more robustly.
source: Conversely, OsSAMS1-knockout mutants, as well as an osein2 mutant defective in ethylene signaling, resisted RDV infection more robustly.
evidence: Supported by infection data in Figure 5

claim: Ethylene plays critical roles in plant development and biotic stress response.
source: Ethylene plays critical roles in plant development and biotic stress response, but the mechanism of ethylene in host antiviral response remains unclear.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ethylene function in plants

claim: The mechanism of ethylene in host antiviral response remains unclear.
source: Ethylene plays critical roles in plant development and biotic stress response, but the mechanism of ethylene in host antiviral response remains unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field

claim: RDV manipulates ethylene biosynthesis in the host plants to achieve efficient infection.
source: Our findings uncover a novel mechanism which RDV manipulates ethylene biosynthesis in the host plants to achieve efficient infection.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all experimental data presented

claim: Pns11 does not affect dynamic association between OsSAMS1 and L-Met.
source: A previous study suggested that enhanced substrate affinity may increase enzyme activity (Toroser et al., 1999); but we found that Pns11 did not alter the affinity of OsSAMS1 to the substrate L-Met or ATP (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by MST assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A

claim: Pns11 does not affect dynamic association between OsSAMS1 and ATP.
source: A previous study suggested that enhanced substrate affinity may increase enzyme activity (Toroser et al., 1999); but we found that Pns11 did not alter the affinity of OsSAMS1 to the substrate L-Met or ATP (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by MST assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 5B

claim: OsSAMS1 exists in a high molecular weight form in RDV-infected rice.
source: We found that OsSAMS1 exists in a high molecular weight form in RDV-infected rice (Figure 2—figure supplement 7), and we propose that the interaction of Pns11 with OsSAMS1 may promote oligomerization of OsSAMS1 to the most active form, which may increase its enzymatic activity and lead to the production of more SAM.
evidence: Supported by gel filtration data in Figure 2—figure supplement 7

claim: The interaction of Pns11 with OsSAMS1 may promote oligomerization of OsSAMS1 to the most active form.
source: We found that OsSAMS1 exists in a high molecular weight form in RDV-infected rice (Figure 2—figure supplement 7), and we propose that the interaction of Pns11 with OsSAMS1 may promote oligomerization of OsSAMS1 to the most active form, which may increase its enzymatic activity and lead to the production of more SAM.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on gel filtration data and enzyme activity results

claim: RDV infection perturbed the expression of several ethylene-response genes such as ERFs.
source: A previous study demonstrated that RDV infection perturbed the expression of several ethylene-response genes such as ERFs (Ethylene Response Factors) (Satoh et al., 2011; Abiri et al., 2017), indicating that ethylene is involved in the interaction between RDV and rice.
evidence: Supported by citations to Satoh et al., 2011 and Abiri et al., 2017

claim: Ethylene is involved in the interaction between RDV and rice.
source: A previous study demonstrated that RDV infection perturbed the expression of several ethylene-response genes such as ERFs (Ethylene Response Factors) (Satoh et al., 2011; Abiri et al., 2017), indicating that ethylene is involved in the interaction between RDV and rice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies showing ERF expression changes

claim: The SAMS enzyme is induced by biotic and abiotic stress.
source: The SAMS enzyme is induced by biotic and abiotic stress and is involved in the regulation of development through the histone and DNA methylation pathway (Roje, 2006; Li et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2013a; Gong et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: SAMS is involved in the regulation of development through the histone and DNA methylation pathway.
source: The SAMS enzyme is induced by biotic and abiotic stress and is involved in the regulation of development through the histone and DNA methylation pathway (Roje, 2006; Li et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2013a; Gong et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: The P6 protein encoded by Cauliflower mosaic virus (CaMV) was found to interact with components of the ethylene-signaling pathway.
source: The P6 protein encoded by Cauliflower mosaic virus (CaMV) was found to interact with components of the ethylene-signaling pathway, and transgenic Arabidopsis expressing P6 became less responsive to ethylene treatment and more resistant to CaMV infection (Geri et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Geri et al., 2004

claim: Transgenic Arabidopsis expressing CaMV P6 became less responsive to ethylene treatment and more resistant to CaMV infection.
source: The P6 protein encoded by Cauliflower mosaic virus (CaMV) was found to interact with components of the ethylene-signaling pathway, and transgenic Arabidopsis expressing P6 became less responsive to ethylene treatment and more resistant to CaMV infection (Geri et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Geri et al., 2004

claim: The ethylene-signaling pathway is required for Turnip mosaic virus (TuMV)-mediated suppression of resistance to the green aphid, Myzus persicae, in Arabidopsis.
source: Another study used ein2 (ethylene insensitive 2) and etr1 (ethylene response 1) mutants and found that the ethylene-signaling pathway is required for Turnip mosaic virus (TuMV)-mediated suppression of resistance to the green aphid, Myzus persicae, in Arabidopsis, and that TuMV may modulate ethylene responses to increase plant susceptibility to viral infection (Casteel et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Casteel et al., 2015

claim: TuMV may modulate ethylene responses to increase plant susceptibility to viral infection.
